title: The Hidden ROI of Caching: Performance Optimization and MIPS Reduction in PBM Engineering
abstract: Caching is often viewed as a response-time optimization, but in PBM engineering it can deliver much deeper value. In high-volume, mainframe-connected environments, smart caching strategies can reduce repeated backend calls, lower MIPS consumption, improve throughput, and strengthen platform resilience. This session explores how caching can evolve from a technical performance tactic into a strategic engineering lever that drives both system optimization and measurable cost savings in PBM platforms. Audience Takeaways * How to identify caching opportunities that reduce mainframe dependency and MIPS usage. * How to balance latency, freshness, and reliability in PBM caching design. * How to position caching as a business-aligned optimization strategy, not just a technical fix.

title: Inside MCP: Live Protocol Messages, Real-Time Flows, and Smarter Agents
abstract: You’ve heard the buzz — now roll up your sleeves and build with it. In this hands-on workshop, you’ll learn exactly how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) works — and you’ll write your own MCP server tool from scratch, then author an Agent that uses it to deliver real-time, context-aware help right inside your dev flow. We’ll break down the raw MCP protocol step by step: • How it streams context between your IDE and Agents • How messages are structured and exchanged • How to wire up an MCP Client to talk to your new tool By the end, you’ll not only understand the protocol — you’ll have built a working MCP server tool and your own Agent that plugs into it to automate tasks, provide better suggestions, and boost your productivity. Bring your curiosity — and your laptop — because you’ll walk away with practical code, a working prototype, and the confidence to build and extend your own MCP-powered tools and Agents.

title: Agents are not Apps: Stop building interfaces, Start building coworkers
abstract: What happens when software stops waiting for input and starts doing the work? We’ve spent decades building apps that sit still until someone clicks a button, fills out a form, or types a prompt. But as AI evolves, the real shift isn’t just in how we interact with software, it’s in what we expect it to do. We’re moving from app-first to agent-first design: from products organized around interfaces to systems organized around autonomous agents that can understand goals, pick up context, make decisions, coordinate with one another, and carry meaningful work forward. This isn’t just chatbot UX or automation with a new coat of paint. The future isn’t richer interfaces for every action. It’s systems that can act on their own, with interfaces reserved for delegation, visibility, and review, and sometimes no interface at all. Whether that means triaging inbound requests, coordinating research, or running a multi-step workflow, the goal isn’t to build better buttons. It’s to build software we can actually employ. In this talk, we’ll break down the core building blocks of agentic systems, including planning, memory, tool use, orchestration, UX, and oversight, and explore the architectural patterns that make them work. We’ll also look at what makes these systems trustworthy: guardrails, human approval where it matters, and clear visibility into what agents are doing and why. The result is a fundamentally different way to think about software: not as passive tools we operate, but as proactive coworkers we collaborate with and delegate to.

title: The node_modules Iceberg: Mysteries Below the Waterline
abstract: What lurks below the tip of the iceberg? Well, if you look at it from the aspect of web and software it is our best friend, the node_modules. Have you ever jumped into your node_modules and looked around to see what the various packages of your packages are? Chances are, no. We don't have time for that...but we should! Let's dive in to the world of transitive dependencies and break down what they are. In this session you will learn what transitive dependencies are, how to list them, the risks they bring, and how to integrate TuxCare's ELS solution to fix them.

title: AI for Java Developers
abstract: AI has become an unavoidable topic in software development, and many Java developers are wondering if they need to learn Python to participate. The answer is no. The Java ecosystem has everything you need to build modern AI applications, and your existing skills carry over more than you might think. This session bridges the gap between traditional Java development and AI. We'll cover the core concepts of AI and large language models in terms familiar to Java developers, then look at what's possible today: chatbots, retrieval augmented generation, recommendation systems, and intelligent agents, all built on the JVM. You'll leave with a clear picture of the Java AI landscape, the confidence that you don't need to switch languages to build production AI features, and a starting point for your first project.

title: Good vibes, smooth payments: Tailoring Stripe to any UI
abstract: It's almost launch day. Your designers have spent months crafting the perfect brand: every color, every typeface, every pixel placed with purpose. The aesthetic is dialed in, and the site looks exactly right. Now your engineers, the ones who've been painstakingly transforming these mockups into code, need to drop in a checkout flow that feels native to the design. No generic-looking payment forms. No jarring style breaks. It has to blend in like it was always there. Is that actually possible? Even when the UI is... a little retro (think GeoCities)? In this talk, I'll walk through different approaches for integrating Stripe Payments into an existing website, from hosted pages to fully embedded, customizable components, and show how far you can push the Stripe Elements Appearance API to match virtually any design system - even one that really shouldn't exist.

title: Writing a Container Runtime in Go
abstract: Every time you run a container on Kubernetes, ECS, or your laptop, something has to create it. But what actually happens between "docker run" and your process running in isolation? In this talk, we'll build a minimal container runtime in Go using the same Linux primitives that power Docker and containerd: namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits, and chroot for filesystem separation. Line by line, we'll construct a working container from nothing but Go and syscalls. You'll walk away understanding what a container actually is at the OS level, why Go is uniquely well-suited for systems tooling like this, and how the infrastructure you deploy to every day really works under the hood. No container experience required.

title: React - Server Components, Suspense, and the new mental model
abstract: React is powering some of the most dynamic digital experiences on the web, and it’s evolving in ways that change how we think about building software. In this session, we’ll explore the ideas shaping modern React, where the server, the browser, and the user experience work together in new and more powerful ways. Instead of focusing on syntax, this talk looks at the bigger shift behind React’s evolution. What does it mean for parts of an app to run before they reach the browser? Why is “loading” no longer just a spinner on the screen? And how do concepts like Server Components and Suspense influence not only performance, but the way we design interactive applications? This session is for anyone curious about where React is headed and why it matters. You’ll get a high-level view of the architectural changes happening behind the scenes, along with the tradeoffs and possibilities they create. Along the way, we’ll uncover how these patterns can lead to faster experiences, cleaner application design, and new ways to think about the future of the web.

title: Squeezing Java Containers: Shrinking Your Kubernetes Footprint with jlink
abstract: Java containers are often bloated, shipping a full JDK and app server to production when your code uses a fraction of it. This session walks through a three-step refactor of the same REST API, from a 523 MB Tomcat WAR to a 121 MB Alpine image with a custom jlink JRE. That's 77% smaller with zero business logic changes, using only standard JDK tooling. We'll cover jdeps, jlink, multi-stage Dockerfile patterns, and the gotchas the tutorials skip: Class Data Sharing, reflection-loaded modules, and what breaks when you add OpenTelemetry. You'll leave with a pattern you can apply to any Java 11+ codebase.

title: Architecting AI in Angular: WebMCP, A2UI, and the Agent Experience
abstract: First we optimized for UX, then DX, and now there's AX - the Agent Experience crashing the party. AI assistants are increasingly showing up to use our apps, and right now most of them get in by screenshotting the DOM and guessing where to click. There's a better way. WebMCP lets your Angular app hand agents a clean set of callable tools, and A2UI lets agents hand back real, reactive UI instead of another wall of chat text. In this session we'll architect an Angular app for this shiny (and slightly experimental) new world. We'll walk through the modes of agent interaction, from quiet background data retrieval to rich, agent-generated interfaces, and look at a few ways to wire WebMCP into Angular through navigator.modelContext. Then we'll bring in A2UI so agents can return reactive component trees that your app renders natively, with your styling and accessibility along for the ride. You'll leave knowing how to register tools, render agent-driven UI, and start thinking about your app's tool surface alongside its visual one. You'll also get a clear-eyed sense of what's production-ready today and what's still gloriously bleeding-edge.

title: CSS as a Game Engine: Building Playful, Stateful Web Experiences Without JS
abstract: What if the browser is already a game console, and CSS is your game engine? In this talk, we'll explore how far you can push the web platform using nothing but HTML and CSS. By treating CSS as a Finite State Machine, we can build surprisingly rich, interactive experiences: movement, hazards, timers, win conditions, even simple game logic. Along the way, we’ll break down the techniques that make this possible and show how they map to real engineering and web development concepts. As part of this session, we'll build a small playable game live on stage, constructed step by step in front of the audience! Beyond the fun, attendees will walk away with new mental models for UI state, fresh ideas for micro‑interactions, and a deeper understanding of how the browser thinks. This talk is ideal for developers who enjoy creative constraints, want to sharpen their understanding of CSS as a state system, or simply want to see the web do something unexpected.

title: How to Test AI Features Before Your Users Do
abstract: LLM-powered features often succeed in demos and still fail in production. A prompt change, model upgrade, or retrieval tweak can quietly reduce answer quality, break grounding, or introduce risky behavior. This talk shows engineers and tech leads how to build a practical eval loop for AI features using the same mindset they already bring to testing software. Using an anonymized internal knowledge assistant as the running example, we will start with a small app that appears to work, then expose three realistic failure modes: unsupported claims, missed key information, and brittle behavior after a change. From there, we will build a lightweight eval suite that turns those failures into repeatable checks. The demo will cover a compact golden dataset, simple scoring patterns, and a regression workflow for prompts, models, and retrieval changes. Attendees will leave able to explain the difference between benchmarks and app evals, compare pass/fail, rubric, and pairwise scoring, implement a small but useful eval dataset, and troubleshoot whether failures come from retrieval, generation, or overall system design.

title: If You’re Not Shipping, You’re Not a Leader
abstract: Leadership is not a calendar of 1:1s. It is whether everything still moves when you leave the room. I learned the hard way, and across four different job families, that kept trying to pull me out of shipping: individual contributor, principal architect, Chief Revenue Officer for an enterprise consulting firm inside companies that move billions of dollars, and now co-founder of a startup whose product sits in other people’s revenue path. Every title got bigger, but the temptation stayed the same - stop shipping, start narrating. This talk is about refusing that trade. How you keep leading from the front instead of the balcony. How you build with the team so you do not become their review queue. How do you instrument work so you can see where it dies, especially when it is stuck on you. How running more than one computer, and putting AI into the path of real work, changes who can cause measurable impact rather than who can write a prettier status update. Finally, how you scale beyond yourself: taste encoded as defaults, handoffs that survive your calendar, a company that still ships when you are on a plane. If your last user-visible change is older than your last status meeting, this one is for you.

title: Utilising the JavaScript Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) for Automated Frontend Lifecycle Management
abstract: This talk explores how to leverage NX's Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) utilities to lvl up frontend code management at scale. We'll dive into strategies for automating frontend maintenance tasks, implementing consistent code patterns, and reducing technical debt through automated code updates. Attendees will learn how to build scalable, automated solutions that can modernize code over the wire, enforce best practices, and streamline development workflows across their entire organization. Learning Objectives 1. Understand how JavaScript AST parsing works and how NX uses this capability. 2. Learn techniques for creating custom AST transformations to automate standard frontend stack updates. 3. Develop strategies for implementing organization-wide code standards through automated transformations.

title: Sociotechnical Platform Engineering
abstract: DevOps practices help reduce friction to production for technologists. Once an application has user traffic, user experience should become a priority, but at what cost? This talk will connect human centered devOps & SRE practices across a value stream to explore how platforms balance developer experience against production stability over time, and how process dependencies factor into overall platform success. this talk will Explore: - How pipelines are value streams - A general-purpose value stream map for platforms - Dependency (wardley) maps for platform processes - Aligning SLIs, SLOs, & SLAs across our platform VSM - Establishing Error Budgets - Chaos Engineering & Complexity Science

title: Thinking Architecturally
abstract: Rich Hickey once said programmers know the benefits of everything and the trade offs of nothing...an approach that can lead a project down a path of frustrated developers and unhappy customers. As architects though, we must consider the trade offs of every new library, language, pattern or approach and quickly make decisions often with incomplete information. How should we think about the inevitable technology choices we have to make on a project? How do we balance competing agendas? How do we keep our team happy and excited without chasing every new thing that someone finds on the inner webs? As architects it is our responsibility to effectively guide our teams on the technology journey. In this talk I will outline the importance of trade offs, how we can analyze new technologies and how we can effectively capture the inevitable architectural decisions we will make. I will also explore the value of fitness functions as a way of ensuring the decisions we make are actually reflected in the code base.

title: The Series Finale Problem: What Happens When Your Brand Makes a Promise You Can't Keep
abstract: Before a single customer signs up, before a product ships, before revenue enters the picture, a startup makes its most consequential decision. Not a hiring decision. Not a pricing decision. Its brand identity decision: the story it chooses to tell the world about what it is and what it promises to deliver. Get that story wrong, and everything that follows is built on an unstable foundation. Customers who arrive expecting one thing while receiving another don't just churn, they leave disillusioned. Worse, they often can't articulate why. Not because they don't know, but because the failure wasn't in the product itself, it was in the gap between what the brand promised and what the experience actually delivered. In this talk, Jeremy Barger examines the Series Finale Problem: the moment when an audience realizes that the story they were hearing was not the story being told. Drawing on a rage-inducing pop culture case study that most attendees will find unexpectedly familiar, Jeremy reveals how a widely beloved brand sustained almost a decade of loyal engagement on the basis of a promise it never intended to keep, and what happened when that became impossible to ignore. The parallel to early-stage startups is precise and actionable. Founders who haven't done the hard work of defining their brand identity before launch routinely build audiences around the wrong promise, and pay for it at exactly the moment momentum should be accelerating. This talk gives founders the framework to catch that misalignment before it becomes irreversible.

title: Building AI Agents in TypeScript with Mastra
abstract: This session is about building AI agents that actually hold up in production using Mastra and TypeScript. We’ll go beyond simple prompt chains and look at how to design multi-step workflows, enforce structured outputs with schemas and build memory systems that don’t fall apart at scale. We’ll also cover how to connect agents to real tools using MCP, handle failures and retries and design systems that can reliably take action instead of just generating text. The focus is on practical patterns, real tradeoffs and what it takes to move from demos to systems that actually work.

title: Baseline Magic: The Art of Intent-Driven CSS
abstract: Modern CSS has entered a new era where we can express intent directly in our styles, treating the latest baseline features as our new fundamentals. In this session, we’ll craft a design piece by piece using ingredients like container queries, layers, and the :has selector. We’ll see how these pieces build on each other to create a cohesive system that is accessible and maintainable by design. You’ll leave with a refreshed perspective on the platform’s potential and the practical foundation needed to start weaving these modern fundamentals into your own projects today.

title: Prickly by Nature: TanStack in the Wild
abstract: The Indio Mountains Research Station (IMRS) is over 40,000 acres of pristine Chihuahuan Desert managed by the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP). The IMRS Biodiversity Explorer is a data-heavy research tool built for students, researchers, and community members alike, integrating iNaturalist observation data, local species data, points of interest on a map, and five years of local historical weather records. It serves three wildly different audiences on a single interface: researchers who speak in taxonomy, students preparing for their first field biology trip, and curious hikers who just want to know what that bird was. The challenge was designing for an ecologist and a casual nature lover without dumbing it down for one or alienating the other. The answer came from my decade in ecology and teaching. In this talk, I'll walk through how domain expertise shaped real technical decisions such as progressive disclosure patterns, dual-mode data views, scientific data modeling, and the architecture choices behind a TanStack app built to serve a genuinely diverse user base. You will leave with a framework for treating user expertise as a design catalyst, and a new appreciation for what non-traditional backgrounds bring to a codebase.

title: The Devil Was Never in the Details: Code, AI, and the Rise of the Deep Generalist
abstract: The rise of AI has quietly elevated one of tech's most undervalued profiles: the Deep Generalist. From LAMP stack administrators who owned everything from bare metal to the application layer, to practitioners today navigating Kubernetes, distributed data pipelines, and observability across cloud providers, the pattern is the same. This talk makes the case for why the seams between systems matter more than the systems themselves, and why AI makes this the Era of the Deep Generalist.

title: Building MARVIN: What Teaching a Non-Technical Marketer to Use MCP Taught Me About AI Adoption
abstract: Over the 2025 holiday break, I built MARVIN, an AI assistant that connects to my email, calendar, Jira, Confluence, and meeting notes through MCP servers. The most surprising lessons came from teaching a non-technical friend in marketing to use it. Within a day, she took a task that typically required 4+ hours and completed it in 30 minutes. In this talk, I'll share practical insights from building and deploying MCP-powered agents in real workflows: - Architecture decisions: How I structured MCP servers for Gmail, Google Calendar, Jira, and other integrations, and where I got it wrong - The "junior intern" pattern: Why treating AI agents like trainable assistants drives real usage - The naming problem: Why "MCP" is a terrible name for mainstream adoption and what we should call it instead - Curiosity over mandates: Why top-down AI adoption fails, and what ground-up adoption looks like I'll walk through 25 minutes of hard-won lessons from building something real, watching people use it, and iterating based on what actually worked.

title: The Death & Resurrection of the IDE: Why Agents Need Semantic Understanding
abstract: In 2026, the narrative has shifted from "browsers will kill the IDE" to "AI agents will make it obsolete." Some of the smartest builders, Aaron Francis among them, haven't opened an IDE since November (his words). So is the IDE actually dying? No. It's evolving. The IDE isn't threatened by agents; it's the only thing capable of keeping agents from becoming black boxes of technical debt. I'll show you why text-based AI sees code as strings, while semantic-aware development tools see code as graphs (AST, data flow, dependencies). Then I'll walk through the real-world cost of that blindness, and show how the next generation of IDEs turns development tools from text editors into an agent's sensory system and orchestration hub. If you've ever had an agent break production, or wondered if you even need an IDE in 2026, this talk is for you. The future is now, old man.

title: Building Intelligent Integration Flows: From Natural Language to Execution with Ballerina
abstract: Enterprise integration is entering a new era, one where systems no longer just follow predefined flows but actively reason about what needs to be done. This session explores the shift from traditional integration pipelines to agentic systems powered by AI. By combining Natural Programming, AI Agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and Model Context Protocol (MCP), we can build systems that understand intent, retrieve context, and execute actions across enterprise environments. With Ballerina as the foundation, we’ll demonstrate how these ideas translate into real-world implementations, where AI orchestrates APIs, interacts with services, and drives business workflows end-to-end. Discover how to design integration platforms where large language models become operational decision-makers, enabling faster development and more intelligent automation.

title: Remote Agents, or: How I Fixed Our Page's Performance Without Really Doing Anything
abstract: Improving performance on a frontend, javascript-heavy, React SPA is an uphill (and often losing) battle. The brunt of the work is a long-tail of missed memoization opportunities, inefficient algorithms, and painstaking fixes. It also just so happens to be an outstanding candidate for agentic engineering. The key piece is that fixes here are verifiable: an agent can run a profile, identify a potential bottleneck, make a code change, and verify that the change improved performance! In this talk I'll describe the architecture of the system I orchestrated to continuously submit verified and ready-to-merge PRs, our findings, and some of the challenges and learnings I came across during the project.

title: The Put That Sh*t On Agent: Building Multi-Agent AI Systems That Actually Talk to Each Other*
abstract: Everyone's building AI agents. But most of them can't talk to each other. They're islands. In this session, we'll walk through a real multi-agent system built with Google's Agent Development Kit and the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol: a wardrobe recommendation app that pulls live weather data, reasons about what to wear, and coordinates across distributed services. You'll see how A2A enables agents to discover each other's capabilities, communicate across deployments, and scale independently, all without tight coupling. We'll also cover how real-time data pipelines (via Conduit) feed your agents, and how to deploy the whole system to Cloud Run. Whether you're building internal tooling or consumer-facing AI features, this talk gives you a battle-tested blueprint for multi-agent architecture that goes beyond the hype.

title: How to Use Scaffolding to Make Your Coding Agents Less Dumb
abstract: Learn how scaffolding can speed up development and reduce your token usage. I'll walk you through the key decisions you should make before sending agents into your codebase. Then I'll demo freeCodeCamp’s new open source create-constellation-app tool.
